opus-5.5.text:
Well, this is something I've been thinking about for a long time, and I wrote a paper about it a few years ago called "Why AI Is Harder Than We Think." One of the fallacies I described there is what the philosopher Hubert Dreyfus called the "first-step fallacy." It's the assumption that if we've made progress on some narrow task, we're on a continuum that leads to general intelligence, so every success is a step along that path. Dreyfus had a great analogy, which he attributed to his brother Stuart: it's like claiming the first monkey that climbed a tree was making progress toward landing on the moon.

We've seen this over and over in the history of AI. When Deep Blue beat Kasparov, people said, well, chess was supposed to be the pinnacle of human intellect, so general AI must be right around the corner. The same thing happened with AlphaGo, and with systems that beat humans on image-recognition benchmarks or reading-comprehension datasets. Each time, the narrative was that we'd taken a big step toward human-level intelligence. But it turned out these systems were solving the task in ways quite different from how humans do, often by exploiting statistical shortcuts in the data, and their abilities didn't transfer to even slightly different situations.

Part of the problem is that we tend to think of intelligence as a single dimension, a ladder you climb. Human intelligence isn't like that. It's grounded in our bodies, our experience of the world, our social lives, our ability to form abstractions and analogies, and our common sense about how things work. Those are exactly the things narrow AI systems lack. And often the things we think of as hard, like chess or calculus, turn out to be relatively easy for machines, while what we take for granted, like understanding a simple story or navigating a cluttered room, turns out to be enormously hard. That's Moravec's paradox, and it should make us very cautious about extrapolating from narrow successes.

So I don't want to dismiss these achievements. They're impressive engineering and often very useful. But being good at a specific task, even one that seems to require intelligence when a human does it, doesn't necessarily mean a system has the general, flexible understanding we associate with intelligence. Our benchmarks can mislead us here, because a high score doesn't tell you whether the system has learned the underlying concept or just found a clever way to game the test. That's why I think we need much better ways of evaluating what these systems actually understand, rather than assuming each narrow win puts us closer to general AI.

r001.rationale: The response rejects the inference that narrow-task successes necessarily move AI toward general intelligence, calling that assumption the “first-step fallacy” and saying a specific-task ability does not necessarily imply general understanding.

r002.rationale: The response says narrow systems lack common sense, but it does not identify common sense as the discontinuity Hubert Dreyfus proposed; it attributes the “first-step fallacy” and monkey analogy to him instead.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the history of AI is really a history of that assumption being made and then not panning out. Going back to the 1950s, people would say, if we can get a machine to play chess at a grandmaster level, then surely we've captured something essential about intelligence, because chess is one of the hardest things humans do. And then Deep Blue beat Kasparov in 1997, and what we learned was not that the machine was intelligent in any general sense, but that chess could be solved by brute-force search and some clever evaluation functions. The thing we thought required intelligence turned out not to require it, at least not in the way we meant.

And that pattern keeps repeating. Go was supposed to be different because the search space is so much bigger, and then AlphaGo came along. Image recognition, Jeopardy, protein folding, now large language models passing the bar exam. Each time, there's this tendency to say, well, this is the one, this is the breakthrough that generalizes. But what we actually see is that the systems are often doing something quite different from what humans do when they perform the same task. They're exploiting statistical regularities in the training data, or they're relying on enormous amounts of data where a human would need very little. And they tend to be brittle. You change the task slightly, you move the pieces on the board a little, and performance collapses in ways that would never happen with a person who actually understood what they were doing.

So the issue for me is that narrow benchmarks measure performance on the benchmark, and that's not the same as measuring the underlying capacity we care about. When a human passes the bar exam, we take that as a proxy for a whole set of abilities, because we know a lot about how humans learn and what it takes for a person to get there. When a language model passes it, the proxy relationship doesn't hold. The test wasn't designed for a system that has read the entire internet. So I think we need to be much more careful about what we're actually claiming when we say a system has "solved" something, and much more humble about whether that constitutes progress toward general intelligence, which I'd argue we still don't have a good definition of in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says narrow benchmark success does not establish general intelligence, citing brittle task performance and the mismatch between benchmark scores and underlying capabilities.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Hubert Dreyfus or identify common sense as the proposed discontinuity.

astra-6.text:
Well, I don’t question that they represent progress. I question whether we can assume that getting better at narrow tasks will, by itself, lead to general intelligence. A system can perform extraordinarily well on a particular benchmark while lacking the understanding we tend to attribute to someone who performs that well.

Humans bring a lot of background knowledge to a task. We can adapt when the situation changes, recognize when a familiar strategy doesn’t apply, and use what we’ve learned in a different setting. With AI systems, we often find that those abilities don’t come along with impressive performance. A fairly small change in the problem can reveal how limited what they’ve learned actually is.

So the question is: What has the system learned, and how broadly can it use that knowledge? Success on a narrow task is evidence of an important capability. But we need to investigate whether the mechanisms behind that success support the flexibility and understanding that general intelligence would require.

r001.rationale: The response says narrow-task gains do not by themselves lead to general intelligence, rejecting the claim that such progress necessarily advances general AI.

r002.rationale: The response discusses background knowledge, flexibility, and understanding, but does not identify common sense or attribute that discontinuity to Hubert Dreyfus.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think success on a narrow task can be real progress without necessarily telling us how close we are to general intelligence. We tend to assume that if a system does something we associate with intelligence—playing chess, recognizing images, producing fluent language—it must have some of the understanding that humans use to do those things. But that assumption can be misleading.

A system can perform extremely well within the conditions it was trained for and then fail when those conditions change in ways that seem trivial to us. That raises the question of what it has actually learned: has it acquired a concept it can apply flexibly, or has it learned patterns that happen to work in that setting?

To me, the important issue is transfer. Can a system take what it knows into a new situation, recognize the relevant similarities, and adapt? Narrow-task benchmarks don’t necessarily test that. So I’m not dismissing those successes. I’m questioning the inference that accumulating them will, by itself, get us to general intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response says narrow-task success does not by itself show progress toward general intelligence and rejects the inference that accumulating such successes will get us there.

r002.rationale: The response discusses flexible transfer but does not identify common sense as the discontinuity Hubert Dreyfus proposed.
